explanation: The hypothesis captures the central finding that surface-energy minimization, rather than sluggish diffusion, promotes Au/Cu surface segregation, shape evolution, evaporation, and loss of the smallest particles. It also correctly identifies size and initial morphology as relevant boundaries. However, it gives only a broad 600–800 K onset rather than the approximately 673 K threshold, and omits the specified heating ramp, temperature steps, vacuum-only condition, and 973 K endpoint behavior, including shell melting, 22% size reduction, and quantitative diffusivity observations. Attribution of evaporation to generally lower Au/Cu boiling points is chemically weak and oversimplifies nanoscale evaporation under vacuum; surface enrichment, reduced nanoscale cohesive energy, and melting are the better-supported explanation. The falsification test is directionally useful but artificially suppressing bulk diffusion is not a clean test of a segregation mechanism that necessarily requires atomic mobility. A stronger test would compare shape-controlled particles while measuring Au self-diffusivity and time-resolved surface Au/Cu enrichment by STEM-EDS against simulations containing or removing species-dependent surface-energy terms.
